The Proximal Bundle Method

Source: R/bundle.R
bundle.Rd

Proximal bundle method for convex non-smooth objectives: subgradients collected at the visited points define a cutting-plane model, a proximal term keeps the step near the stability center, and convergence is tested on the optimality estimate \(\lVert p \rVert^2 + \alpha\), built from the aggregate subgradient \(p\) and its linearization error \(\alpha\), and not on a single subgradient, which does not vanish at a kink.

Usage

bundle(
  criterion = crit_stationary(),
  t0 = 1,
  t_min = 1e-10,
  t_max = 1e+10,
  accept_fraction = 0.1,
  bundle_size = 20,
  qp_iters = 500,
  qp_tol = 1e-12,
  maxit = 500,
  max_eval = Inf,
  verbose = FALSE,
  refresh = 10,
  keep_trace = FALSE
)

Arguments

criterion

The stopping rule. Defaults to crit_stationary(1e-8), read on the optimality estimate \(\lVert p \rVert^2 + \alpha\).

t0

Initial value of the proximal parameter \(t\), expressed as a step length on the parameter scale and not as a bare multiplier; see Details. Defaults to 1.

t_min, t_max

Bounds on it, so that a run of null steps or a run of serious ones cannot drive it to zero or to infinity. The defaults are 1e-10 and 1e10.

accept_fraction

Fraction of the predicted decrease that a step must actually deliver to be accepted, in \((0, 1)\). Defaults to 0.1.

bundle_size

Largest number of linearizations kept; when a new one would exceed it, the oldest are replaced by the aggregate. Defaults to 20.

qp_iters, qp_tol

Effort spent on the subproblem: at most this many accelerated projected-gradient steps, stopping when the weights move by less than qp_tol. The defaults are 500 and 1e-12.

maxit

Maximum iterations. Defaults to 500.

max_eval

Maximum objective evaluations. Defaults to Inf, which sets no evaluation budget, so the run stops on the criterion or on maxit. Set a finite value to cap the cost of a run.

verbose

Report progress? Defaults to FALSE.

refresh

Report every this many iterations. Defaults to 10.

keep_trace

Store the iteration path? Defaults to FALSE.

Value

An S7 object of class Bundle, inheriting from optimizer(), to be handed to minimize().

Behavior at a kink

Near the minimum of \(\lvert x \rvert\) the evaluated subgradient is \(\pm 1\). The gradient norm seen by a descent method therefore stays large, the line search finds no acceptable step, and the run stops at the minimizer without meeting its stopping rule, whatever the tolerance. On the median example below, bfgs() reaches the median and reports converged = FALSE.

The bundle method tests no single subgradient. It keeps a collection of them, from the points that it has visited, and builds the piecewise-linear model \(\max_j \{ f_j + g_j'(x - x_j) \}\), the largest of the linearizations. Such a model represents a kink well, as the meeting point of two linearizations. At the minimum of \(\lvert x \rvert\) the bundle holds subgradients near \(+1\) and near \(-1\), and \(0\) is a convex combination of them, which is the statement that \(0\) lies in the subdifferential.

The step solves $$\min_d\ \max_j \{ -\alpha_j + g_j'd \} + \frac{1}{2t}\lVert d \rVert^2,$$ where \(\alpha_j \ge 0\) measures how far linearization \(j\) lies below the objective at the current point, and the quadratic term keeps the step inside the region where the model is trusted. The minimizer is \(d = -t\,p\), with \(p\) the aggregate subgradient and \(\alpha\) the aggregate linearization error. The value of the piecewise-linear model at \(d\), \(v = -(t\lVert p \rVert^2 + \alpha) \le 0\), is the predicted decrease, which the acceptance test below reads.

crit_stationary() reads a related but different quantity, the optimality estimate \(\lVert p \rVert^2 + \alpha\). Both vanish at a solution, but \(-v\) contains the factor \(t\), and \(t\) is halved at every null step, so \(-v\) can fall below any tolerance because the trust parameter has shrunk and not because the point is stationary. A run that stopped on \(-v\) would then report convergence at a point where the model still has a large aggregate subgradient. The optimality estimate omits the factor \(t\) and does not depend on the size of the trust parameter.

Serious steps and null steps

A trial point is accepted, making a serious step, only if the decrease that it delivers is at least the fraction accept_fraction of the predicted decrease. This plays the role of the Armijo condition in a line search: without a required fraction, a sequence of ever smaller improvements could be accepted although it does not converge to a minimizer.

A rejected trial point still contributes its subgradient to the bundle, which improves the model at the next iteration. Such an iteration is a null step, and a run with many null steps is refining the model of a kink. Both counts appear in the message of the result, as in 8 serious, 14 null.

t is halved after a null step and doubled after a serious one, within t_min and t_max. Kiwiel's rule chooses the factor from a curvature estimate and performs better; the rule implemented here is simpler and bounded.

The trust parameter t0

The step is \(d = -t\,p\), so with a bare t the length of the first step would be proportional to the size of the gradient. On a steep objective that step lands where the objective is enormous, each null step halves t while the gradients collected there are larger still, and the run can spend its whole budget on rejected steps.

When the largest absolute component of the gradient at the starting point exceeds 1, t0 is therefore divided by that component, so that the largest coordinate of the first step has size t0; otherwise t0 is used as it is. This is the normalization of a line search that starts at 1 along a unit direction, and t_min and t_max are scaled in the same way. A larger t0 suits a problem whose optimum is far away, and a smaller one a problem on which the model is accurate only nearby.

Should a subgradient overflow anyway, which an objective that grows fast enough can produce, the run stops with a message instead of spending its budget on a subproblem whose matrix contains an infinity.

Bounded memory

Without a limit the bundle grows indefinitely. When a new linearization would make it exceed bundle_size, the oldest linearizations are replaced by the aggregate, the affine function defined by the solution of the subproblem at the current stability center. Discarding them would lose their information and can stall the method; the aggregate retains a summary of that information in one element.

Convexity requirement

The theory is for convex \(f\), where the linearization errors \(\alpha_j\) are non-negative automatically. On a non-convex objective they can be negative and are clipped at zero. The method still runs and usually works, but the convergence guarantee no longer applies: a negative error means that \(f\) lies below one of its own linearizations, and setting the error to zero discards that information.

Subgradients

Supply gr. Without it the package computes the gradient by finite differences, which is accurate wherever \(f\) is differentiable, that is, almost everywhere. A difference taken across a kink is not a subgradient, and the model is then built from a number that does not correspond to any linearization of \(f\).

References

Kiwiel, K. C. (1990). Proximity control in bundle methods for convex nondifferentiable minimization. Mathematical Programming 46, 105–122.

Mäkelä, M. M. (2002). Survey of bundle methods for nonsmooth optimization. Optimization Methods and Software 17, 1–29.

See also

prox_grad() for the non-smooth case where a proximal operator is available, nelder_mead() and compass() for the derivative-free methods, crit_stationary() for the default rule of this method.

Examples

bundle()
#> <optimizer> proximal bundle
#>   stop when : stationarity < 1e-08
#>   budgets   : maxit 500, evaluations Inf
#>   settings  : t0 = 1, t_min = 1e-10, t_max = 1e+10, accept_fraction = 0.1, bundle_size = 20, qp_iters = 500, qp_tol = 1e-12

# The median is the minimizer of a sum of absolute deviations: the
# objective has a kink at every observation, and one of them is the answer.
set.seed(1)
y <- rnorm(101)
f <- function(p) sum(abs(y - p))
g <- function(p) -sum(sign(y - p))

r <- minimize(bundle(), f, par = 0, gr = g)
c(bundle = r@par, median = median(y))
#>     bundle     median 
#> 0.07456498 0.07456498 
abs(r@par - median(y))     # 8e-16
#> [1] 1.151856e-15
r@message                  # how many trials were accepted
#> [1] "8 serious, 14 null"

# The aggregate subgradient goes to zero at the kink, whereas the
# subgradient computed by g just beside it has norm 1.
r@gradient
#> [1] 2.767786e-13
abs(g(r@par - 1e-9))
#> [1] 1

# A descent method lands on the same point and cannot certify it.
d <- minimize(bfgs(criterion = crit_grad()), f, par = 0, gr = g)
c(par = d@par, converged = d@converged)
#>        par  converged 
#> 0.07456498 0.00000000 

# The kink lies along a diagonal. The bundle method and the simplex reach the
# minimum; the random-direction pattern search (the default of compass())
# comes close, whereas a coordinate search stops at a wrong point.
ff <- function(p) abs(p[1] + p[2]) + 0.1 * sum(p^2)
gg <- function(p) c(sign(p[1] + p[2]), sign(p[1] + p[2])) + 0.2 * p
c(bundle      = minimize(bundle(), ff, c(1, 0.5), gr = gg)@value,
  nelder_mead = minimize(nelder_mead(), ff, c(1, 0.5))@value,
  compass     = minimize(compass(), ff, c(1, 0.5))@value)
#>       bundle  nelder_mead      compass 
#> 8.206869e-09 9.439361e-17 2.114785e-03 

# A gradient rule is rejected, since this method declares no gradient.
try(minimize(bundle(criterion = crit_grad()), f, par = 0, gr = g))
#> Error : The stopping rule needs gradient, which proximal bundle does not provide.
#>   Choose a criterion that this optimizer can evaluate, or a method that provides it.
